newsitem.title: USA: Lawyer says U.S. Army tank engineer "not a spy".
newsitem.headline: Lawyer says U.S. Army tank engineer "not a spy".

text.p: An Army tank engineer suspected of divulging U.S. military secrets to Israel is not a spy, but merely the victim of a huge misunderstanding, his lawyer said on Thursday.
"David Tenenbaum is not a spy. He has never been engaged in espionage. He has never given classified information to the Israelis," attorney Martin Crandall told Reuters in a telephone interview.

The Pentagon said on Thursday that Tenenbaum, 39, was removed from his job with pay at the U.S. Army Tank, Automotive and Armaments Command (TACOM) in Warren, Michigan, after the FBI last week began investigating whether he had divulged classfied information on U.S. weapons programmes to Israeli liaison officers over the past 10 years.
Tenenbaum has not been arrested and no charges have been filed against him.

"He has been placed on administrative leave. His employee badge and his parking permit have been revoked pending the outcome of the investigation," Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon said on Thursday.
The FBI disclosed on Wednesday that federal agents had seized computers, financial records and other documents related to armour systems from Tenenbaum's suburban Detroit home.

In an affidavit filed in U.S. District Court in Detroit, the FBI said Tenenbaum admitted that he disclosed Patriot missile countermeasures data, ceramic armour data, armour test and survivability data and unreleasable classified information on the Bradley Fighting Vehicle and the "Humvee" off-road vehicle to Israeli officers.
The affidavit also said Tenenbaum admitted that he had taken documents labeled "For Official Use Only" and "Secret" to his home in Southfield, Michigan.

The TACOM research and development centre where Tenenbaum works provides design, engineering and support services for the Army's tracked and wheeled vehicle programmes, ranging from the Humvee to the top-of-the line M1-A2 Abrams tank.
But Crandall said Tenenbaum's contacts with Israeli liaison officers assigned to TACOM never involved classified or secret information.
"Anything that he ever exchanged with anybody was legitimate and authorised," Crandall said. "Anything that was in his house was justifiably there."
Crandall added that he was working with the FBI investigators to "unravel this web of misinformation."

He contends that a Defence Investigative Service agent misinterpreted and overreacted to Tenenbaum's answers to questions in a polygraph test that was being administered as part of an upgrade in the engineer's security clearance.
Crandall said he wants "vindication" of Tenenbaum in the form of an "affirmative statement" that he never engaged in any wrongdoing.
"This certainly feels like a Richard Jewell situation," Crandall said, referring to the investigation of the Atlanta security guard in last July's Olympic bombing.
